However, I haven't found an example that mimics the problems I have trying to make distributions from the 'extraDistr' package available to my nimble model. In particular, I would like to include the negative hypergeometric distribution in my model (rnhyper,dnhyper,qnhyper,pnhyper).   Any advice on how to implement distributions from other packages would be very helpful.    Thank you.

messages.body_plain:
hi David,

You could of course implement the distribution of interest by directly coding the mathematical calculations in user-defined nimbleFunctions, as you say.
If you want to be able to call out to code provided by `extraDistr`, you might want to look into using `nimbleRcall` or `nimbleExternalCall` to
be able to call out to R or C/C++ code from within a nimbleFunction and thereby avoiding having to write up the calculations yourself.
There is help information via R's help system: `help(nimbleRcall)` and `help(nimbleExternalCall)`.

Happy to discuss further.

-chris

messages.body_plain:
Hello developers,

Quick question on an error I'm getting during a compileNimble() call of some new functionality I'm trying to add to the BayesNSGP package I've developed with Daniel Turek.

Everything in R seems to be working, but in converting to C++ I'm getting the following errors:

P_2_tau_eq_constant_sigma_eq_constant_Sigma_eq_constantIso_sparse_eq_bumpPlusSparse_mu_eq_constant_likelihood_eq_gp2Scale_nfCode.cpp:3633:14: error: no matching function for call to 'rcFun_R_GlobalEnv26'
Interm_165 = rcFun_R_GlobalEnv26(Interm_158, Interm_159, 100, 1, 2, 3, Interm_160, Interm_161, Interm_162, Interm_163, Interm_164);
             ^~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~
P_2_tau_eq_constant_sigma_eq_constant_Sigma_eq_constantIso_sparse_eq_bumpPlusSparse_mu_eq_constant_likelihood_eq_gp2Scale_nfCode.cpp:3375:20: note: candidate function not viable: no known conversion from 'NimArr<1, double>' to 'NimArr<2, double> &' for 2nd argument
NimArr<2, double>  rcFun_R_GlobalEnv26 ( NimArr<2, double> & ARG1_dists_, NimArr<2, double> & ARG2_coords_, double ARG3_N_, double ARG4_d_, double ARG5_n1_, double ARG6_n2_, double ARG7_r0_, NimArr<2, double> & ARG8_bumpLocs_, NimArr<2, double> & ARG9_rads_, NimArr<2, double> & ARG10_ampls_, NimArr<2, double> & ARG11_shps_ )  {
                   ^

My guess is that this has to do with my trying to pass a one-column matrix, which (despite my best efforts) seems to still be treated as a double(1) by nimble. Any advice? Also, how can I look at the generated C++ code to try to identify the various "Interim_XX" variables?

Thanks,
Mark Risser

messages.body_plain:
Hi Mark,

You can find the generated code in tempdir().

Can you send the code for the coords argument, as called from one nimbleFunction to another nimbleFunction that takes arguments (dists, coords, N, d, etc.).  (You can choose a function name for the C++ if you provide the name argument to nimbleFunction.)

If you have something like coords[1:n, 1] and you want it to stay as a matrix, try coords[1:n, 1, drop=FALSE].

If you have an expression that is returning a vector when you want a one-column matrix, you could do:
my_result <- matrix(nrow = n, ncol = 1, init=FALSE)
my_result[ , 1] <- (some expression)

HTH
Perry

messages.body_plain:
Hi David,

As far as using nimbleRcall or nimbleExternalCall, the latter will generally be faster, as there is overhead in calling out to R. So if the density will be called many times (as it would be in many algorithms, including MCMC), it may be worthwhile to set up the C/C++ code for the distribution of interest. And in fact, since extraDistr::dnhyper (and the 'r','p','q' functions) calls directly out to C++, it should 'just' be a matter of using the underlying C++ code in the source code for the extraDistr package.

You definitely need the `x` argument. That doesn't appear directly in the density in a nimble model (it's actually the left-hand side of the declaration in the nimble model code), but behind the scenes the model code is transformed so that the first argument to the density is `x`.

A couple other comments about your nimbleRcall:
- in general we recommend just working with doubles rather than integers, as nimble model calculations are all done with doubles. There is no loss of accuracy. We mention this in the help info for `registerDistributions`, though we should probably also mention it in Section 12.2 of the User Manual.
- I presume your returnType should be of dimension 0 not dimension 1.

I'm not quite sure what you mean by "as the model develops".

-chris

messages.body_plain:
Hi David,

I haven't looked closely but nimble expects the first argument of the 'r' function is named 'n' and gives the number of samples desired when generating from the distribution -- see Section 12.2 of the manual. So I think you'll need to rename the 'n' parameter of your user-defined distribution to be something different to avoid argument name conflicts.

-chris

messages.body_plain:
Hi Mark,

I think you're running into one of the awkward corners of nimble, that it is difficult to maintain a singleton dimension when you want to. Workarounds include:

- making a variant of sparseKernel for the case d = 1, for which coords is a vector.  You can use definition-time if-then-else to branch to the different cases of model declarations during model building.

- padding coords with an extra column, passing it with "1:(d+1)" if needed, and adding an extra argument to indicate whether it has been padded.

We have plans to make this better but they are currently behind our plans working towards a major release.

Perry

Great thanks, that makes sense.   I think I may have achieved that with the code below (using urn terminology for white balls and black balls) but it is producing some odd results. There is no variance in the posterior distribution for the neghyp parameters but the random sample generating seems to be working well.

rm(list=ls())

library(nimble)
library(extraDistr)

dnhype2<-nimbleRcall(function(x= double(0,default=1), n = double(0, default = 1), m = double(0, default = 1), r = double(0, default = 1), log=integer(0,default=0)){}, Rfun="dnhyper",returnType=double(0))

rnhype2<-nimbleRcall(function(nn= double(0,default=1), n = double(0, default = 1), m = double(0, default = 1), r = double(0, default = 1)){}, Rfun="rnhyper",returnType=double(0))

dnhype <- nimbleFunction(
  run = function(x= double(0), white = double(0, default = 1), black = double(0, default = 1), failures = double(0, default = 1),log = integer(0, default = 0)) {
    returnType(double(0))
    Prob<-dnhype2(x,white,black,failures)
  return(Prob)
  })

rnhype <- nimbleFunction(
  run = function(n= double(0,default=1), white = double(0, default = 1), black = double(0, default = 1), failures = double(0, default = 1)) {
    returnType(double(0))
    return(rnhype2(1,white,black,failures))
  })

nsites<-1000
testG<-rnhyper(nsites,50,50,3) # 'data'
testG[seq(2,nsites,by=2)]<-NA

data<-list(testG=testG)
constants<-list(nsites=nsites)
nhyper_code <- nimbleCode({

  # failurs cannot be smaller than white
  black~dunif(11,100)
  white~dunif(11,100)
  failures~dunif(1,10)

   for (i in 1:nsites){

     testG[i]~dnhype(black,white,failures)
   }
})

  # Inital values
  testGinit<-rep(NA,nsites)
  testGinit[is.na <http://is.na>(testG)]<-11

  # best to initialize failures at 1, so that no inconsistencies arise with initial values
  inits <- function() list(black=50, white=50,failures=1,testG=testGinit)

  initsValues <- inits

  # Parameters to monitor

  params <- c("black","white","failures","testG")

  # MCMC
  ni <- 25000
  nb <- 5000

  ## run nimble
  nhype <- nimbleMCMC(
    code = nhyper_code,

    data=data,
    constants=constants,

    inits = initsValues,
    monitors = params,
    nburnin = nb,
    niter = ni,

    thin=100,
    samplesAsCodaMCMC = TRUE
  )

  library(coda)
  library(mcmcplots)

  mcmcplot(nhype)

  hist(nhype[,seq(2,nsites,by=2)])
  hist(testG)
  hist(nhype[,3])

Your guess is correct: If N is passed as a constant, then it will not be sampled, and gradients will not be calculated for it.

On Tue, Apr 4, 2023 at 5:01 PM SILIZ4 <lizotte...@gmail.com> wrote:

>

For instance, let's say I have a custom function to which I pass the size of the input N as a parameter. Will nimble attempt to compute the derivative with respect to N, or it will automatically ignore it as it's not sampled? I would guess the latter, but I just wanna validate since it could cost many unnecessary operations.

> Le mardi 28 mars 2023 à 09:46:07 UTC-4, Daniel Turek a écrit :
> > Thanks for using nimbleHMC, and also sending your question.
> >
> > A very short answer would be: it's not apparent offhand what's going wrong, and to really figure it out, we'd need a reproducible example.  If you'd prefer to send that (model code, data, etc) off-list, then that's no problem at all.
> >
> > No, only populating half of the values in the adjacency matrix is not a problem.  The HMC sampler will only access and use the values in the parts you access inside the for-loops.
> >
> > That said: you said that you "only iterate on the lower half of it.... the rest of the matrix is not initialized because of this", but a quick inspection of the for-loops in your code makes it appear like (instead) you only iterate on the upper half of it.  So, perhaps there's something going wrong here (providing values for the wrong half of the adjacency matrix), that might be causing this problem.  It might be worth a look at that.
> >
> > Regarding your second question: If by "ignores their gradient evaluation" you mean "ignores the gradient evaluation of the custom-written nimble functions entirely", then no, gradients of these functions are not ignored, but rather algebraically derived (via automatic differentiation), while using the values of the constant arguments you provided.  Or, if by "ignores their gradient evaluation", you mean the "ignores the partial derivatives of the custom-written nimble functions w.r.t. the constant-valued arguments", then yes, automatic differentiation is not applied to the constant-valued arguments, much the same as it would not be applied to an argument which is hard-coded as a number (say, 5).  The gradient (partial derivatives) of the function are only calculated w.r.t. continuous-valued non-constant arguments, as is necessary for HMC sampling.
> >
> > Cheers, keep at it,
> > Daniel
> >
> >
> >
> >

messages.body_plain:
Question about specifying monitors. In my function <https://github.com/qureshlatif/QSLpersonal/blob/master/R/RunNimbleParallel.R>, I am specifying monitors using  modelConf$addMonitors(parameters). It appears that monitors are added for parameters that contain all strings in `parameters`. For example, if I have two parameters appearing in my model, "sigma" and "tvar_sigma", and I include "sigma" as an element in `parameters`, monitors will be added for both "sigma" and "tvar_sigma" because both contain the string "sigma". Is this the way adding monitors is intended to function with Nimble, and is there a way to change this functionality to only add monitors for parameters whose names match exactly the elements in `parameters`?

On Tuesday, January 24, 2023 at 7:17:29 AM UTC-7 Daniel Turek wrote:
> Queresh, good question.  The short answer is there's no built-in mechanism for doing this in NIMBLE's MCMC, but there have been two attempts at documenting the procedure you're asking about.  I think the second of these is a little better, but please take a look at both:
>
> http://danielturek.github.io/public/restartingMCMC/restartingMCMC.html
> https://danielturek.github.io/public/saveMCMCstate/saveMCMCstate.html
>
> Let me know if you have any questions about this.
>
> Cheers,
> Daniel
>

> > I am starting to thinking a little more about how to build on the work documented in this thread, one piece of functionality that would be nice to add is to be able to resume sampling from where one has left off if interrupted (e.g., due to a power outage or automatic Windows update). Is it possible to save the entire MCMC sampling state to the hard drive such that one can resume sampling from that point rather than starting from scratch?

Quresh, thanks for the question as always.

Bottom line, what you described should not be the case.  There is no "matching of all strings to all variables" that takes place when adding monitors to an MCMC configuration.  I believe something else must be causing whatever you're witnessing.

One possibility, I see that in your function <https://github.com/qureshlatif/QSLpersonal/blob/master/R/RunNimbleParallel.R>, you first call:

modelConf <- configureMCMC(model, thin = nt)

It's possible that "tvar_sigma" is being added as a default monitor by configureMCMC -- unless otherwise specified, configureMCMC assigns monitors to all top-level non-data stochastic nodes in a model.  Then, later, when you use conf$addMonitors to add a monitor for "sigma", you now have monitors on both "sigma" (added manually) and "tvar_sigma" (added initially by configureMCMC by default).  Is this possibly the case?

I'll also point out functions:

conf$resetMonitors()       ## remove all current monitors
conf$setMonitors(params)   ## remove all current monitors, and add monitors for params

If this still doesn't resolve your question, can you send a reproducible example demonstrating the problem?

Thanks,
Daniel

Hi NIMBLE community,

I am trying to understand the outputs of my multistate capture-recapture model, and I feel I have exhausted all other troubleshooting options. I hope you can assist!

In summary, I had been trying to troubleshoot oddly low population size estimates when I became confused by the categorical sampling of the state process matrix. When I monitor the underlying deterministic parameters and calculate out the probabilities per iteration of sampling (i.e. essentially build the state matrix for each iteration), it appears that certain transitions should be very likely (e.g. 2>2). However, the monitored z-matrix does not suggest this pattern and rather state 7 is the more likely state in most instances. There are no issues in the z-matrix for individuals that have known states assigned the question relates to instances where sampling occurs.

What I am trying to understand is how the sampling process could produce a z-matrix that is so different from what the calculated probability matrix suggest. The sampling never behaves aberrantly (i.e. unallowed transitions (e.g. 2>1) never occur) so I don't think it is some sort of indexing or referencing issue.  Is there something obvious that I am missing here?

For context, the purpose of the model is to estimate abundance of a species across N-occasions while accounting for subpopulation-, time-, and individual-dependent covariates. It becomes quite complex and lengthy so I don't want to burden you with detail on the data, model structure and initialization. The important components I think are the following:

1) nind = N (real individuals) + N (pseudo-individuals) # data augmentation with zeros
2) all individuals start in latent state 1 within occasion 1 (dummy occasion)
3) a z.init matrix is provided which has all unknown states as 2 (assume still alive) for real individuals and 1 (not yet entered) for pseudo-individuals
4) inputted data are y (observation matrix); z (state matrix, with NAs for unknown states)
5) Not all state transitions are possible and probabilities are outlined below along with the likelihood portion of the nimbleCode.

# -------------------------------------------------------------------
for (i in 1:nind){
    # Define probabilities of state S(t+1) given S(t)
    for (t in 1:(n.occasions-1)){
      ps[1,i,t,1] <- (1-gamma[t]) * (1-intro[t])
      ps[1,i,t,2] <- gamma[t]
      ps[1,i,t,3] <- intro[t] * (1-gamma[t])
      ps[1,i,t,4] <- 0
      ps[1,i,t,5] <- 0
      ps[1,i,t,6] <- 0
      ps[1,i,t,7] <- 0
      ps[2,i,t,1] <- 0
      ps[2,i,t,2] <- s[i,t] * (1-tran[t])

      ps[2,i,t,6] <- s[i,t] * tran[t]
      ps[2,i,t,7] <- (1-s[i,t]) * (1-r[i,t])
      ps[3,i,t,1] <- 0

      ps[3,i,t,3] <- 0
      ps[3,i,t,4] <- 0
      ps[3,i,t,5] <- 0
      ps[3,i,t,6] <- 0
      ps[3,i,t,7] <- 0
      ps[4,i,t,1] <- 0
      ps[4,i,t,2] <- 0
      ps[4,i,t,3] <- 0
      ps[4,i,t,4] <- 0
      ps[4,i,t,5] <- 0
      ps[4,i,t,6] <- 0
      ps[4,i,t,7] <- 1
      ps[5,i,t,1] <- 0
      ps[5,i,t,2] <- 0
      ps[5,i,t,3] <- 0
      ps[5,i,t,4] <- 0
      ps[5,i,t,5] <- 0
      ps[5,i,t,6] <- 0
      ps[5,i,t,7] <- 1
      ps[6,i,t,1] <- 0
      ps[6,i,t,2] <- 0
      ps[6,i,t,3] <- 0
      ps[6,i,t,4] <- 0

      ps[7,i,t,4] <- 0
      ps[7,i,t,5] <- 0
      ps[7,i,t,6] <- 0
      ps[7,i,t,7] <- 1

      # Define probabilities of O(t) given S(t)
      po[1,i,t,1] <- 0
      po[1,i,t,2] <- 0
      po[1,i,t,3] <- 0
      po[1,i,t,4] <- 0
      po[1,i,t,5] <- 0

      po[2,i,t,3] <- 0
      po[2,i,t,4] <- 0

      po[2,i,t,6] <- 1-p[i,t]
      po[3,i,t,1] <- 0

      po[3,i,t,3] <- 0
      po[3,i,t,4] <- 0
      po[3,i,t,5] <- 0

      po[4,i,t,1] <- 0

      po[4,i,t,3] <- 1
      po[4,i,t,4] <- 0
      po[4,i,t,5] <- 0
      po[4,i,t,6] <- 0
      po[5,i,t,1] <- 0
      po[5,i,t,2] <- 0
      po[5,i,t,3] <- 0
      po[5,i,t,4] <- 1
      po[5,i,t,5] <- 0
      po[5,i,t,6] <- 0
      po[6,i,t,1] <- 0
      po[6,i,t,2] <- 0
      po[6,i,t,3] <- 0
      po[6,i,t,4] <- 0
      po[6,i,t,5] <- 1
      po[6,i,t,6] <- 0
      po[7,i,t,1] <- 0
      po[7,i,t,2] <- 0
      po[7,i,t,3] <- 0
      po[7,i,t,4] <- 0
      po[7,i,t,5] <- 0
      po[7,i,t,6] <- 1
    } #t
  } #i

  # Likelihood
  for (i in 1:nind){
    z[i,1] <- 1  # Define latent state at first capture
    for (t in 2:n.occasions){
      # State process: draw S(t) given S(t-1)
      z[i,t] ~ dcat(ps[z[i,t-1], i, t-1, 1:7])
      # Observation process: draw O(t) given S(t)
      y[i,t] ~ dcat(po[z[i,t], i, t-1, 1:6])
    } #t
  } #i

I am happy to provide a reproducible example if helpful. I just thought I would put the question out there first to see if there was something obvious that I was missing or if anyone has ever encountered something like this.

Thanks in advance,
Robin

messages.subject: Re: Categorical sampler and z-matrix outputs
messages.subject_clean: Categorical sampler and z-matrix outputs
messages.body_plain:
Robin, good question.  The categorical sampler functions in a reasonably straightforward manner.  Say:

z[1] ~ dcat(prior)
z[2] ~ dcat( f(z[1]) )
y[1] ~ dcat( g(z[1] )

Then the (categorical) sampling of z[1] will evaluate the (proportional) conditional distribution: p( Z[1]   |   z[2], y[1] )

for all possible values of Z[1].  For the value Z[1] = a, this conditional distribution is proportional to:

p(z[2] | Z[1]=a) * p(y[1] | Z[1] = a),

where both terms come from the categorical distributions in the model.

This is a long-winded way of saying: the categorical sampler samples directly from the full conditional (posterior) distribution of each z[] term.  So, to explain the behavior you're seeing, despite what the elements of the transition matrix might suggest, the terms from the likelihood (the observed values of y), and the downstream latent z values (which themselves are informed by the downstream data) must suggest a different distribution for the latent states you're monitoring.

I have reasonable confidence that the categorical sampler is functioning correctly, for a few reasons including that it's not a new addition, and it's been tested in many different situations. That said, there's always a chance that something funny is going on with your model.  If you really want to get to the bottom of it, since you have the samples of the latent z's, you can recreate (calculate yourself) the exact (proportional) distribution that the categorical sampler is sampling from, and see what the actual (proportional) probabilities are.  This might be insightful regarding what's informing the latent state values, and why.

I hope this helps somewhat.  Maybe someone else will have a more practically helpful response.

Cheers, have a nice weekend,
Daniel

messages.body_plain:
Hello,

I got some naive questions about the control of the RW sampler and wonder about the details.

First, when should we choose:
1. log==TRUE
2. reflective==TRUE
3. change adaptFactorExponent = 0.5 or 0.8 or other values?

Second, I noticed that the target acceptance rate is fixed to 0.44 (see https://github.com/cran/nimble/blob/master/R/MCMC_samplers.R). How can we change it to 0.234 to check the effect on the estimation results?

Thank you for the NIMBLE and the forum for discussion!

Keith

messages.subject: Re: Control of RW sampler
messages.subject_clean: Control of RW sampler
messages.body_plain:
Great questions, Keith.

1. log=TRUE is helpful when the parameter domain is strictly positive (like for variance / standard deviation parameters) and also potentially has non-trivial posterior density near to 0.  This serves to expand the unit interval [0,1] to the entire space of negative reals, and also remove the lower boundary, so sampling might work much better.  So, for example for standard deviation terms, where the posterior density might be close to 0.

2. reflective = TRUE when the parameter domain is bounded on an interval, for example a probability bounded in [0,1], with non-trivial posterior density near to one/both boundaries.  This makes the MH sampling "reflect" proposals off of the boundaries, so no proposal is "out of bounds".  So you might use this for a probability parameter, where the posterior is near to either 0 or 1.

3. Setting adaptFactorExponent to other values is experimental, we don't have much good guidance about what works well in different situations.  Higher values (anything positive is valid) will make the adaptation decay quickly, that is, the scale of proposals will quickly begin to change very little between adaptation cycles, and lower values (closer to 0) mean that adaptation of the proposal scale will attenuate very slowly, and continue to make (potentially large) changes for many adaptation cycles.  So high values will "stabilize" the adaptation of the proposal scale quickly, but perhaps it won't have sufficient time to adapt to a good value, while low values will make the adaptation span many MCMC iterations.  As I said, there's no good guidance on what will work better in different situations.

You're right, for all of the options, it appears the RW sampler target acceptance rate is hard-coded to be 0.44.  We could make this an option very easily, if that's useful.  Otherise, your best bet is to copy the RW sampler code, change this value (or make it into an option), define your custom sampler (maybe named "RW2", to be vague), and then add this new sampler to the MCMC configuration using addSampler.

Hope this helps,
Daniel

messages.body_plain:
I don't know if it can be related to Robin's issue, but I recently experienced some strange behaviour with the categorical sampler. It was outputting values that should have had strictly zero probability, as their prior probability was zero. I tried to understand what was happening; the problem seems to arise from extremely small values of the likelihood, leading to very small *unnormalized* posterior categorical probabilities.

Replacing the categorical sampler with the slice one solved the problem for me. Robin, would it be possible in your case to try that too?

I plan to report reproducible details within a couple of weeks. Nimble version is the latest.

Cheers,
Luca

On 7 April 2023 15:57:53 UTC, Daniel Turek <danie...@gmail.com> wrote:
>Robin, good question.  The categorical sampler functions in a reasonably
>straightforward manner.  Say:
>
>z[1] ~ dcat(prior)
>z[2] ~ dcat( f(z[1]) )
>y[1] ~ dcat( g(z[1] )
>
>Then the (categorical) sampling of z[1] will evaluate the (proportional)
>conditional distribution: p( Z[1]   |   z[2], y[1] )
>
>for all possible values of Z[1].  For the value Z[1] = a, this conditional
>distribution is proportional to:
>
>p(z[2] | Z[1]=a) * p(y[1] | Z[1] = a),
>
>where both terms come from the categorical distributions in the model.
>
>This is a long-winded way of saying: the categorical sampler samples
>directly from the full conditional (posterior) distribution of each z[]
>term.  So, to explain the behavior you're seeing, despite what the elements
>of the transition matrix might suggest, the terms from the likelihood (the
>observed values of y), and the downstream latent z values (which themselves
>are informed by the downstream data) must suggest a different distribution
>for the latent states you're monitoring.
>
>I have reasonable confidence that the categorical sampler is functioning
>correctly, for a few reasons including that it's not a new addition, and
>it's been tested in many different situations. That said, there's always a
>chance that something funny is going on with your model.  If you really
>want to get to the bottom of it, since you have the samples of the latent
>z's, you can recreate (calculate yourself) the exact (proportional)
>distribution that the categorical sampler is sampling from, and see what
>the actual (proportional) probabilities are.  This might be insightful
>regarding what's informing the latent state values, and why.
>
>I hope this helps somewhat.  Maybe someone else will have a more
>practically helpful response.
>
>Cheers, have a nice weekend,
>Daniel

> >Robin, good question.  The categorical sampler functions in a reasonably
> >straightforward manner.  Say:
> >
> >z[1] ~ dcat(prior)
> >z[2] ~ dcat( f(z[1]) )
> >y[1] ~ dcat( g(z[1] )
> >
> >Then the (categorical) sampling of z[1] will evaluate the (proportional)
> >conditional distribution: p( Z[1]   |   z[2], y[1] )
> >
> >for all possible values of Z[1].  For the value Z[1] = a, this conditional
> >distribution is proportional to:
> >
> >p(z[2] | Z[1]=a) * p(y[1] | Z[1] = a),
> >
> >where both terms come from the categorical distributions in the model.
> >
> >This is a long-winded way of saying: the categorical sampler samples
> >directly from the full conditional (posterior) distribution of each z[]
> >term.  So, to explain the behavior you're seeing, despite what the elements
> >of the transition matrix might suggest, the terms from the likelihood (the
> >observed values of y), and the downstream latent z values (which themselves
> >are informed by the downstream data) must suggest a different distribution
> >for the latent states you're monitoring.
> >
> >I have reasonable confidence that the categorical sampler is functioning
> >correctly, for a few reasons including that it's not a new addition, and
> >it's been tested in many different situations. That said, there's always a
> >chance that something funny is going on with your model.  If you really
> >want to get to the bottom of it, since you have the samples of the latent
> >z's, you can recreate (calculate yourself) the exact (proportional)
> >distribution that the categorical sampler is sampling from, and see what

> >

> >

Hello All,
This thread has been helpful to me in getting started to fit a negative hypergeometric (thanks to Chris P on another thread). I have adapted the code posted here formulating the negative hypergeometric in the attached code.   The density function appears to recover data generating values.  However, the random number generation doesn't seem to generate posterior distributions for a missing data value.  I have attached code with a simple example that demonstrates the random number generation works as expected in R but can only produce '0' as an outcome in nimble.   I can't figure out why this is the case.

Using other inits values on z is not so easy, because I sent you a simplified code. Real code is extremely complex... But to clarify, your proposal is rewriting the MS code to avoid having to update the missing values and supply only the non-missing values as data. Isn’t it?
> >

> > Best regards
> >

> > De: nimble...@googlegroups.com <nimble...@googlegroups.com> En nombre de Chris Paciorek

> > Hi Jose,
> >
> >
> >
> > I think the issue is with the initial values, combined with how NIMBLE handles predictive node sampling by default. (Where the predictive nodes are those that have no dependencies and are simply sampled from their prior distributions conditional on the current parameter values at a given MCMC iteraation; in your case this is the missing y's.)
> >
> >
> >
> > You start all the z's at 3. In the initial iterations. It looks like in the initial iterations (during burnin) the psi and r values get close to 1 and get stuck there.
> >
> > I think if you start the z's at a mix of values, things will look much better.
> >
> >
> >
> > I think this stickiness is probably made much worse by the fact that the MCMC is also sampling the predictive nodes. And given how many of them there are, this probably causes a lot of posterior dependence. It's likely hard for the z's to mix because they are related to all of those predictive nodes, and the current values of those predictive nodes in any given MCMC iteration strongly constrains the z's.
> >
> >
> >
> > Given this, if you take a little time to rewrite the model to exclude the predictive nodes, this should greatly speed up the mixing (and the pure computational time of the MCMC). You would need to change the indexing of y[i,t] to be something like:
> >
> >
> >
> > for(j in 1:nObserved)
> >
> >  y[j] ~ dcat(p[z[ivec[j]],tvec[j],1:3])
> >
> >
> >
> > where "ivec" and "tvec" map from 1:nObserved to the values of "i" and "t" for the observed y's. If you needed samples of the unknown y's you can easily do that with the MCMC output if you save samples of the z's.
> >
> >
> >
> > As far as the difference with JAGS and BUGS, I believe that JAGS (and this may be true for BUGS too) is smarter than NIMBLE's default handling of predictive nodes -- in particular when updating parameters of the model, I suspect JAGS is having those updates not depend on the predictive nodes.
> >
> > Having our default MCMC configuration be smarter about predictive nodes is something we've talked about in some detail before on the development team but just haven't had time to improve yet. In part, this is because the user configurability of our MCMC means we have to make sure that if users modify a default MCMC configuration that ignores the predictive nodes when sampling the parameters, it doesn't create an incorrect MCMC.  I'll bring it up again for the team to think about.
> >
> >
> >
> > -chris
> >
> >

Subject: Re: Run parallel chains and update model

Quresh, thanks for the question as always.

Bottom line, what you described should not be the case.  There is no "matching of all strings to all variables" that takes place when adding monitors to an MCMC configuration.  I believe something else must be causing whatever you're witnessing.

One possibility, I see that in your function <https://link.edgepilot.com/s/c8b2dbdd/2p2fpinWa0mxg0CFTVbZCg?u=https://github.com/qureshlatif/QSLpersonal/blob/master/R/RunNimbleParallel.R>, you first call:

modelConf <- configureMCMC(model, thin = nt)

It's possible that "tvar_sigma" is being added as a default monitor by configureMCMC -- unless otherwise specified, configureMCMC assigns monitors to all top-level non-data stochastic nodes in a model.  Then, later, when you use conf$addMonitors to add a monitor for "sigma", you now have monitors on both "sigma" (added manually) and "tvar_sigma" (added initially by configureMCMC by default).  Is this possibly the case?

I'll also point out functions:

conf$resetMonitors()       ## remove all current monitors

conf$setMonitors(params)   ## remove all current monitors, and add monitors for params

If this still doesn't resolve your question, can you send a reproducible example demonstrating the problem?

Thanks,

Daniel

> Question about specifying monitors. It appears that monitors are added for parameters that contain all strings in `parameters`. For example, if I have two parameters appearing in my model, "sigma" and "tvar_sigma", and I include "sigma" as an element in `parameters`, monitors will be added for both "sigma" and "tvar_sigma" because both contain the string "sigma". Is this the way adding monitors is intended to function with Nimble, and is there a way to change this functionality to only add monitors for parameters whose names match exactly the elements in `parameters`?

Dear NIMBLE community,

I've encountered a cryptic error whilst exploring the wonderful world of nimbleFunctions. Briefly, I'm trying to create a nimbleFunction to calculate a 2D array of species richness for site-survey combinations, based off of a 4D array ( species x site x survey x plot within site) of species expected abundances.

The function I've written works before compilation, but when I attempt to compile, I get a cryptic error about a parsing failure. Reproducible example shown below, with the error message highlighted.

When I modify the nimbleFunction to remove the na.rm = TRUE argument, I get a different error, which I also include below.

I'm still pretty shaky with nimbleFunctions, so hopefully I'm missing something obvious. Any help is much appreciated!

Cheers,

Neil

library(nimble)

nsp <- 10
nsite <- 20
max_period <- round(runif(nsite, 2, 10))
max_plot <- array( round(runif( nsite * max(max_period, na.rm = TRUE), 2, 6)),
                   dim = c( nsite, max(max_period, na.rm = TRUE)))
# 4D array of expected abundances - species x site x survey period x plot within site
lambda <- array( runif( nsp * nsite * max(max_period, na.rm = TRUE) * max(max_plot, na.rm = TRUE), 0.2, 5),
                 dim = c( nsp, nsite, max(max_period, na.rm = TRUE), max(max_plot, na.rm = TRUE)))

Runique <- nimbleRcall(
  function( x = double( 4 )){},
  Rfun = 'unique',
  returnType =  double(2))

calc_site_richness <- nimbleFunction(
  run = function(
    lambda = double(4),
    nsp = integer(0),
    nsite = integer(0),
    max_period = integer(1),
    max_plot = integer(2)){

    species_id <- array( NA, dim = c( nsp, nsite, max(max_period, na.rm = TRUE), max(max_plot, na.rm = TRUE)))
    richness_site <- array( NA, dim = c(nsite, max(max_period, na.rm = TRUE)))
    for( s in 1:nsite) {
      for( t in 1:max_period[s]){
        richness_site[s, t] <- length( Runique( species_id[ 1:nsp, s, t, 1:max_plot[s, t]]))
        for( j in 1:max_plot[s, t]){
          for( h in 1:nsp){
            if( lambda[ h, s, t, j] > 1){
              species_id[ h, s, t, j] <- h
            }
          }
        }
      }
    }
    return(richness_site)
    returnType(double(2))
  }
)

# works
calc_site_richness( lambda = lambda,
                    nsp = nsp,
                    nsite = nsite,
                    max_period = max_period,
                    max_plot = max_plot)

# Won't compile - cryptic error:
# Error in parse(text = nimDeparse(code), keep.source = FALSE) :
#   <text>:1:9: unexpected '='
# 1: pairmax(=
#              ^
C_calc_site_richness <- compileNimble( calc_site_richness )

messages.body_plain:
hi Neil,

A couple things here:

1) The nimble compiler can't handle the `na.rm=TRUE` argument to `max`. By providing it, that causes some downstream issues that I won't go into.
One work-around would be to replace the NAs in `max_plot` and `max_period` with some fixed negative number as a placeholder and take out the `na.rm=TRUE`.
Another (probably better) option is to compute those two maxes in R and pass in as two additional args to `calc_site_richness` and use those args to define the dimensions of the matrices.

2) Having gotten past that, the other problem that will occur is that by using scalar `s`, and `t`, you are passing a 2-dimensional input to `Runique`.
So `Runique` should have  `x = double( 2)` instead of ` x = double(4)`.

-chris

messages.body_plain:
Hi David,

I haven't fully worked through what is happening on the C++ side, but I think the issue is that `white`, `black` and `failures` need to be integer-valued. It's fine if they are of double type (nimble stores all numeric values internally in a model as doubles), but your prior doesn't constrain them to be integers. As a result nimble's samplers just treat them as continuous random variables and propose (and accept) non-integer values. Then I think that in the compiled `rnhyperg`, the behavior you see comes from trying to use a non-integer-valued value in `length = maxx-minx+1` or in `(minx+1):maxx` (since `maxx` is just `black`) or in passing non-integer values into `dnhyperg`.

I think you'll need a prior that treats the parameters as integer-valued and then nimble should assign a sampler that respects that.

-chris

> > > I think the issue is with the initial values, combined with how NIMBLE handles predictive node sampling by default. (Where the predictive nodes are those that have no dependencies and are simply sampled from their prior distributions conditional on the current parameter values at a given MCMC iteraation; in your case this is the missing y's.)
> > >
> > >
> > >
> > > You start all the z's at 3. In the initial iterations. It looks like in the initial iterations (during burnin) the psi and r values get close to 1 and get stuck there.
> > >
> > > I think if you start the z's at a mix of values, things will look much better.
> > >
> > >
> > >
> > > I think this stickiness is probably made much worse by the fact that the MCMC is also sampling the predictive nodes. And given how many of them there are, this probably causes a lot of posterior dependence. It's likely hard for the z's to mix because they are related to all of those predictive nodes, and the current values of those predictive nodes in any given MCMC iteration strongly constrains the z's.
> > >
> > >
> > >
> > > Given this, if you take a little time to rewrite the model to exclude the predictive nodes, this should greatly speed up the mixing (and the pure computational time of the MCMC). You would need to change the indexing of y[i,t] to be something like:
> > >
> > >
> > >
> > > for(j in 1:nObserved)
> > >
> > >  y[j] ~ dcat(p[z[ivec[j]],tvec[j],1:3])
> > >
> > >
> > >
> > > where "ivec" and "tvec" map from 1:nObserved to the values of "i" and "t" for the observed y's. If you needed samples of the unknown y's you can easily do that with the MCMC output if you save samples of the z's.
> > >
> > >
> > >
> > > As far as the difference with JAGS and BUGS, I believe that JAGS (and this may be true for BUGS too) is smarter than NIMBLE's default handling of predictive nodes -- in particular when updating parameters of the model, I suspect JAGS is having those updates not depend on the predictive nodes.
> > >
> > > Having our default MCMC configuration be smarter about predictive nodes is something we've talked about in some detail before on the development team but just haven't had time to improve yet. In part, this is because the user configurability of our MCMC means we have to make sure that if users modify a default MCMC configuration that ignores the predictive nodes when sampling the parameters, it doesn't create an incorrect MCMC.  I'll bring it up again for the team to think about.

Keith, in the function definition of your RW2 sampler, find the line that says:

ccList <- mcmc_determineCalcAndCopyNodes(model, target)

and try changing it to:

ccList <- nimble:::mcmc_determineCalcAndCopyNodes(model, target)

GIve that a try.

Daniel

On Tue, Apr 11, 2023 at 6:04 PM Keith Lau <genw...@gmail.com> wrote:
> Thank you, Daniel. They are very informative in understanding how to use the settings.
> For the acceptance rate, I followed your instruction and then ran into a problem. First, I copied sampler_RW  function, named it as RW2, and modified it with "optimalAR <- 0.234". Next, I did a loop to set up conf$addSampler(paste("lambda[",k,",",i,"]",sep=""), type = "RW2"), where conf is from configureMCMC(). However, buildMCMC(conf) showed an error message:
> Error in mcmc_determineCalcAndCopyNodes(model, target) :
>   could not find function "mcmc_determineCalcAndCopyNodes"
>
> I think I must miss some important steps. I looked up the manual but still not sure how to solve it.
>
> Keith
> Daniel Turek 在 2023年4月8日 星期六凌晨2:46:55 [UTC+8] 的信中寫道：

> > Great questions, Keith.
> >
> > 1. log=TRUE is helpful when the parameter domain is strictly positive (like for variance / standard deviation parameters) and also potentially has non-trivial posterior density near to 0.  This serves to expand the unit interval [0,1] to the entire space of negative reals, and also remove the lower boundary, so sampling might work much better.  So, for example for standard deviation terms, where the posterior density might be close to 0.
> >
> > 2. reflective = TRUE when the parameter domain is bounded on an interval, for example a probability bounded in [0,1], with non-trivial posterior density near to one/both boundaries.  This makes the MH sampling "reflect" proposals off of the boundaries, so no proposal is "out of bounds".  So you might use this for a probability parameter, where the posterior is near to either 0 or 1.
> >
> > 3. Setting adaptFactorExponent to other values is experimental, we don't have much good guidance about what works well in different situations.  Higher values (anything positive is valid) will make the adaptation decay quickly, that is, the scale of proposals will quickly begin to change very little between adaptation cycles, and lower values (closer to 0) mean that adaptation of the proposal scale will attenuate very slowly, and continue to make (potentially large) changes for many adaptation cycles.  So high values will "stabilize" the adaptation of the proposal scale quickly, but perhaps it won't have sufficient time to adapt to a good value, while low values will make the adaptation span many MCMC iterations.  As I said, there's no good guidance on what will work better in different situations.
> >
> > You're right, for all of the options, it appears the RW sampler target acceptance rate is hard-coded to be 0.44.  We could make this an option very easily, if that's useful.  Otherise, your best bet is to copy the RW sampler code, change this value (or make it into an option), define your custom sampler (maybe named "RW2", to be vague), and then add this new sampler to the MCMC configuration using addSampler.
> >
> > Hope this helps,
> > Daniel
> >
> >
> >

On Tuesday, April 11, 2023 at 7:40:12 PM UTC-6 Chris Paciorek wrote:
> Hi David,
>
> I haven't fully worked through what is happening on the C++ side, but I think the issue is that `white`, `black` and `failures` need to be integer-valued. It's fine if they are of double type (nimble stores all numeric values internally in a model as doubles), but your prior doesn't constrain them to be integers. As a result nimble's samplers just treat them as continuous random variables and propose (and accept) non-integer values. Then I think that in the compiled `rnhyperg`, the behavior you see comes from trying to use a non-integer-valued value in `length = maxx-minx+1` or in `(minx+1):maxx` (since `maxx` is just `black`) or in passing non-integer values into `dnhyperg`.
>
> I think you'll need a prior that treats the parameters as integer-valued and then nimble should assign a sampler that respects that.
>
> -chris

> > > > I think the issue is with the initial values, combined with how NIMBLE handles predictive node sampling by default. (Where the predictive nodes are those that have no dependencies and are simply sampled from their prior distributions conditional on the current parameter values at a given MCMC iteraation; in your case this is the missing y's.)
> > > >
> > > >
> > > >
> > > > You start all the z's at 3. In the initial iterations. It looks like in the initial iterations (during burnin) the psi and r values get close to 1 and get stuck there.
> > > >
> > > > I think if you start the z's at a mix of values, things will look much better.
> > > >
> > > >
> > > >
> > > > I think this stickiness is probably made much worse by the fact that the MCMC is also sampling the predictive nodes. And given how many of them there are, this probably causes a lot of posterior dependence. It's likely hard for the z's to mix because they are related to all of those predictive nodes, and the current values of those predictive nodes in any given MCMC iteration strongly constrains the z's.
> > > >
> > > >
> > > >
> > > > Given this, if you take a little time to rewrite the model to exclude the predictive nodes, this should greatly speed up the mixing (and the pure computational time of the MCMC). You would need to change the indexing of y[i,t] to be something like:
> > > >
> > > >
> > > >
> > > > for(j in 1:nObserved)
> > > >
> > > >  y[j] ~ dcat(p[z[ivec[j]],tvec[j],1:3])
> > > >
> > > >
> > > >
> > > > where "ivec" and "tvec" map from 1:nObserved to the values of "i" and "t" for the observed y's. If you needed samples of the unknown y's you can easily do that with the MCMC output if you save samples of the z's.
> > > >
> > > >
> > > >
> > > > As far as the difference with JAGS and BUGS, I believe that JAGS (and this may be true for BUGS too) is smarter than NIMBLE's default handling of predictive nodes -- in particular when updating parameters of the model, I suspect JAGS is having those updates not depend on the predictive nodes.
> > > >
> > > > Having our default MCMC configuration be smarter about predictive nodes is something we've talked about in some detail before on the development team but just haven't had time to improve yet. In part, this is because the user configurability of our MCMC means we have to make sure that if users modify a default MCMC configuration that ignores the predictive nodes when sampling the parameters, it doesn't create an incorrect MCMC. > hi Neil,
>
> A couple things here:
>
> 1) The nimble compiler can't handle the `na.rm=TRUE` argument to `max`. By providing it, that causes some downstream issues that I won't go into.
> One work-around would be to replace the NAs in `max_plot` and `max_period` with some fixed negative number as a placeholder and take out the `na.rm=TRUE`.
> Another (probably better) option is to compute those two maxes in R and pass in as two additional args to `calc_site_richness` and use those args to define the dimensions of the matrices.
>
> 2) Having gotten past that, the other problem that will occur is that by using scalar `s`, and `t`, you are passing a 2-dimensional input to `Runique`.
> So `Runique` should have  `x = double( 2)` instead of ` x = double(4)`.
>
> -chris
>

messages.body_plain:
I think using Rscript, that could be a good strategy. You'll likely want to write a file of R code, say `run_chain.R`) that implements a single chain and saves the results in a chain-specific file.
The R file should take an ID as an argument, using syntax like:

  args <- commandArgs(TRUE)
  chainID <- as.numeric(args[1])

Then in your main R script, you can use parLapply (as seen in our parallelization example <https://r-nimble.org/nimbleExamples/parallelizing_NIMBLE.html>) to invoke a function where that function uses system2 to invoke the file with the ID of the chain.

run_MCMC_allcode <- function(seed) {
  system2(paste("Rscript run_chain.R", seed)
}

Let me know if any of that is not clear.

It's clunky, I know. We are working on the memory limitations as part of an overhaul of the compiler and model-building systems, but that's a long-term project.

You could also experiment with using `nimble:::clearCompiled`(see here <https://r-nimble.org/html_manual/cha-progr-with-models.html#clearing-and-unloading-compiled-objects>) to clear out compiled objects that might be holding onto a lot of memory, but as I played a
bit with that for a simple case, it didn't seem to be effective in terms of freeing up memory, so I'm not sure how well it would work for you.

-chris

> > > > Hi Henry,
> > > >
> > > > This is a tricky issue.  We have built two features to attempt to reduce memory use, but still it seems that objects evade R's garbage collection.  This may be because we have a lot of reference class objects and environments, creating potentially closed loops of referenced objects.  The two features are:
> > > >
> > > >   nimbleOptions(clearNimbleFunctionsAfterCompiling = TRUE) # This can modestly reduce memory use
> > > >
> > > >   nimble:::clearCompiled(model) # This attempts to clear all compiled content for the project related to model and to unload the on-the-fly compiled shared library used for it.
> > > >
> > > > However I tried both of these and they don't resolve the issue you're reporting.  It's something we'll have to look into more.   We have worked on this in the past but this doesn't look like good behavior.
> > > >
> > > > Here are some potential workarounds.
> > > >
> > > > You could within each loop use system2() to call Rscript and launch a self-contained process.  This would make sense if you really need to do the full nimble building and compilation each time.
> > > >
> > > > If you are really re-using the same model structure, you could build and compile just once and then simply re-assign data values.  e.g.
> > > > Cmodel$y <- some_other_values
> > > > then re-run your already-compiled MCMC.
> > > >
> > > > If in your simulations you need models of different sizes or different setups of what is data (observed vs unobserved), it gets trickier but it is still possible to build and compile just once and re-use those objects.  For example you can configure-build-compile a full set of samplers for all nodes (including, atypically, data nodes) and then control the sampler order in a particular run of the MCMC to include some samplers and omit others.  In that way, you can make some nodes handled like data and some like unobserved on a run-by-run basis.  If that sounds like something you need and it is too imprecisely described here, please holler again and we could go into more detail.
> > > >
> > > > Will one of those approaches help you?
> > > >
> > > > -Perry

The model is somewhat complex and a little slow to build/compile, but it behaves reasonably well for a single run on one dataset. However, when I try to repeatedly fit the model for the simulation study, R rapidly grows in its memory usage until it overwhelms my system's resources.
> > > > >
> > > > > I've created what I think is a minimum working example of the phenomenon I'm encountering. The first loop below aligns with my understanding of how R's memory use works (ie, removing variables and doing garbage collection releases memory). The second loop shows the confusing behavior I'm encountering with nimble. I would expect the memory usage to stay flat as in the first case, but it seems to grow linearly with each iteration. > > > > >
> > > > > Thanks,

messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

I'm trying to compile a function that creates a correlation matrix from a vector of correlations. The function I wrote is:

nim_cor_mat <- nimbleFunction(
  run = function(n_dim = double(0), rho = double(1)) {
    returnType(double(2))
    cor_mat <- diag(n_dim)
    cor_mat[R_lower.tri(cor_mat)] <- rho
    cor_mat <- cor_mat + t(cor_mat)
    diag(cor_mat) <- 1
    return(cor_mat)
  }
)

where I've used nimbleRcall to create the function R_lower.tri:

R_lower.tri <- nimbleRcall(
  function(x = double(2)) {},
  Rfun = "lower.tri",
  returnType = double(2)
)

The function runs fine in R but when I try to compile it says:

Error: Error, wrong number of indices provided for cor_mat[Interm_1027].
 This occurred for: cor_mat[Interm_1027]
 This was part of the call:  cor_mat[Interm_1027] <- ARG2_rho_

I'm not sure where I went wrong so figured I'd post here!

Cheers,

Matt

Hi Matt,
I think the indexing (logical matrix) in
cor_mat[R_lower.tri(cor_mat)]
is not supported in the nimble compiler.

I think it will be easiest to do it internally, without using lower.tri, something like

i_rho <- 1
for(j in 1:(n-1))
  for(i in (j+1):n {
    cor_mat[i,j] <- rho[i_rho]
    cor_mat[j,i] <- rho[i_rho]
    i_rho <- i_rho + 1
  }

-Perry

messages.subject: LGCP on simulated example
messages.subject_clean: LGCP on simulated example
messages.body_plain:
Hi fellow NIMBLE developers,

I’m trying to fit a log-Gaussian Cox process (LGCP) on a simulated dataset, but I’m experiencing problems with MCMC divergence. I’m attempting to use a custom likelihood function. I tried to have separate samplers for each parameter (commented out in my code below), but that also did not work. I would be grateful if you would be willing to take a look and share any thoughts on where/how I might improve my approach. Please let me know if you have any questions!

Thank you very much for your time.

Best,
Zhihan

Below is a reproducible example in R.

Importing libraries:

```{r}

set.seed(42)

library(nimble)

library(ggplot2)

library(fields)  # for rdist

library(glue)

library(dplyr)

library(sf)

library(sp)

library(spatstat)

library(reshape2)

#install RandomFieldsUtils if necessary, it has been removed from CRAN

#install.packages(("https://cran.r-project.org/src/contrib/Archive/RandomFieldsUtils/RandomFieldsUtils_1.2.5.tar.gz"), repos=NULL, type="source")

library(RandomFieldsUtils)

#install RandomFields if needed

#install.packages(("https://cran.r-project.org/src/contrib/Archive/RandomFields/RandomFields_3.3.14.tar.gz"), repos=NULL, type="source")

library(RandomFields)

```

Generate a simulated dataset:

```{r}

sampled_process <- rLGCP("exp", function(x, y){0.1 * x - 0.1 * y + 1},

           var=1, scale=4,

           win = owin(c(-10, 10), c(-10, 10)))

plot(sampled_process)

```

I’m using an exponential covariance function:

```{r}

expcov <- nimbleFunction(run = function(dists = double(2), phi = double(0), sigma = double(0)) {

    returnType(double(2))

    n <- dim(dists)[1]

    m <- dim(dists)[2]

    sigma2 <- sigma*sigma

    result <- sigma2*exp(-dists/phi)

    return(result)

})

```

Defining observed points (obs_pts), knots and integration points (int_pts):

```{r}

obs_pts <- as.data.frame(sampled_process)

knots_xs <- seq(from = -10, to = 10, length.out = 10)

knots_ys <- seq(from = -10, to = 10, length.out = 10)

knots <- expand.grid(knots_xs, knots_ys)

colnames(knots) <- c("x", "y")

int_xs <- runif(500, min=-10, max=10)

int_ys <- runif(500, min=-10, max=10)

int_pts <- data.frame(cbind(int_xs, int_ys))

colnames(int_pts) <- c("x", "y")

```

```{r}

n_uof = nrow(obs_pts)

n_sim = nrow(int_pts)

n_knots <- nrow(knots)

# defining covariate values for regression

# in this case, the x-y coordinates themselves are the covariates

covs <- as.matrix(obs_pts)

sim_covs <- as.matrix(int_pts)  # sim stands for “simulation”

# distance matrices

knots_dists <- rdist(knots, knots)

observed_pts_vs_knots_dists <- rdist(obs_pts, knots)

integration_pts_vs_knots_dists <- rdist(int_pts, knots)

```

I’m using knots to reduce the computational cost (following this paper https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC3712798/).

Basically, instead of directly sampling the value of the GP on the observed data points, I first sample the value of the GP on the knots (which are much fewer than the number of data points) and then interpolate the value of the GP on the observed data points using Gaussian conditioning formulas.

```{r}

code <- nimbleCode({

  beta0 ~ dnorm(0, sd = 100)

  beta1 ~ dnorm(0, sd = 100)

  beta2 ~ dnorm(0, sd = 100)

  sigma ~ dinvgamma(1, 1)

  XB[1:n_uof] <- beta0 + beta1*covs[,1] + beta2*covs[,2]

  XB_int[1:n_sim] <- beta0 + beta1*sim_covs[,1] + beta2*sim_covs[,2]

  knots_cov[1:n_knots, 1:n_knots] <- expcov(knots_dists[1:n_knots, 1:n_knots], phi=4, sigma=sigma)

  observed_pts_vs_knots_cov[1:n_uof, 1:n_knots] <- expcov(observed_pts_vs_knots_dists[1:n_uof, 1:n_knots], phi=4, sigma=sigma)

  integration_pts_vs_knots_cov[1:n_sim, 1:n_knots] <- expcov(integration_pts_vs_knots_dists[1:n_sim, 1:n_knots], phi=4, sigma=sigma)

  gp_on_knots[1:n_knots] ~ dmnorm(knots_mean[1:n_knots], cov=knots_cov[1:n_knots, 1:n_knots])

  gp_on_observed_pts[1:n_uof] <- observed_pts_vs_knots_cov[1:n_uof, 1:n_knots] %*% inverse(knots_cov[1:n_knots, 1:n_knots]) %*% asCol(gp_on_knots[1:n_knots])

  gp_on_integration_pts[1:n_sim] <- integration_pts_vs_knots_cov[1:n_sim, 1:n_knots] %*% inverse(knots_cov[1:n_knots, 1:n_knots]) %*% asCol(gp_on_knots[1:n_knots])

  integ <- (area / n_sim) * sum(exp(XB_int[1:n_sim] + gp_on_integration_pts[1:n_sim]))

  })

```

Constructing nimbleModel:

```{r}

Rmodel <- nimbleModel(

  code,

  data = list(),

  inits = list(

    beta0 = 0,

    beta1 = 0,

    beta2 = 0,

    sigma = 1,

    gp_on_knots = numeric(n_knots)

  ),

  constants = list(

    sim_covs = sim_covs,

    covs = covs,

    area = 400,  # 20 * 20

    n_uof = n_uof,

    n_sim = n_sim,

    knots_mean = numeric(n_knots),

    knots_dists = knots_dists,

    observed_pts_vs_knots_dists = observed_pts_vs_knots_dists,

    integration_pts_vs_knots_dists = integration_pts_vs_knots_dists,

    n_knots = n_knots

  )

)

```

```{r}

Rmodel$initializeInfo()

```

Defining custom log likelihood:

I’m using a block sampler for all parameters instead of adding a separate sampler for each parameter - the second approach doesn’t seem to work (for example, the posterior samples for sigma look like they are from the prior).

```{r}

llFun <- nimbleFunction(

  setup = function(model) { },

  run = function() {

    ll <- sum(model$XB + model$gp_on_observed_pts) - model$integ

    returnType(double())

    return(ll[1])

  }

)

RllFun <- llFun(Rmodel)

mcmcConf <- configureMCMC(Rmodel, nodes = NULL, monitors = c("beta0", "beta1", "beta2", "sigma", "gp_on_knots"))

# this ensures that gp_on_knots is monitored alongside of other nodes, but also makes sure that no default samplers are assigned (we are adding a custom sampler just below)

# adding custom samplers

mcmcConf$addSampler(target = c("beta0", "beta1", "beta2", "sigma", "gp_on_knots"),

                    type = "RW_llFunction_block",

                    control = list(llFunction = RllFun, includesTarget = F))

# mcmcConf$addSampler(target = "beta1", type = "RW_llFunction",

#                     control = list(llFunction = RllFun, includesTarget = FALSE))

#

# mcmcConf$addSampler(target = "beta2", type = "RW_llFunction",

#                     control = list(llFunction = RllFun, includesTarget = FALSE))

#

# mcmcConf$addSampler(target = "sigma", type = "RW_llFunction",

#                     control = list(llFunction = RllFun, includesTarget = FALSE))

#

# mcmcConf$addSampler(target = "gp_on_knots", type = "RW_llFunction_block",

#                     control = list(llFunction = RllFun, includesTarget = FALSE))

mcmcConf$printSamplers()

Rmcmc <- buildMCMC(mcmcConf)

comp_model <- compileNimble(Rmodel)

comp_MCMC <- compileNimble(Rmcmc)

```

```{r}

mcmcConf$getUnsampledNodes()

```

```{r}

comp_MCMC$run(niter = 10000)

```

Here’s the code I’ve written for plotting the trace plots:

```{r}

samples <- as.matrix(comp_MCMC$mvSamples) %>% as.data.frame()

n_samples <- nrow(samples)

# trace plot for beta0, beta1 and beta2

ggplot() +

  geom_line(aes(x=1:n_samples, y=samples[, 1]), color="red") +   # beta0

  geom_line(aes(x=1:n_samples, y=samples[, 2]), color="green") +   # beta1

  geom_line(aes(x=1:n_samples, y=samples[, 3]), color="blue") +   # beta2

  xlab("Number of samples") +

  ylab("Value")

# trace plot for the value of GP on a few knots (1st to 10th)

melted_samples <- melt(cbind(1:n_samples, samples[, 4:14]), id.vars="1:n_samples")

colnames(melted_samples)[1] <- "index"

ggplot() +

  geom_line(data=melted_samples, aes(x=index, y=value, color=variable)) +

  xlab("Number of samples") +

  ylab("Value") +

  theme(legend.position="none")

# trace plot for sigma

ggplot() + geom_line(aes(x=1:n_samples, y=samples[, ncol(samples)]))

```

messages.body_plain:
Hello All,

I am working on an integrated species distribution model built from citizen science data. The model uses a zero-inflated Poisson distribution with separate regressions defining variation in abundance (lambda) and occupancy (psi). Both regressions also include a CAR term to account for spatial autocorrelation amongst cells in which surveys took place. The model code is below, and I have attached scripts for both generating a simulated dataset and using  a subset of Ebird and BBS data as trial example.

The model runs but I consistently get low ESS values for at least one of the regression parameters when using the the simulated data set, usually the intercept term for the abundance regression (beta0, ESS ~10 with 10k interations and 10 thinning). When using real data, I get low ESS for most if not all regression coefficients (<100 with 10k iterations and 10 thinning).

 I have attempted to use blocking according to this paper (https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1002/ece3.6053), but with little success. I have also tried allowing the model to run longer, but ESS remains so low that I asume it indicates something is wrong.

If anyone has any suggestions or thoughts on what could be causing the problem, it would be greatly appreciated.

code <- nimbleCode({
  ### State Process
  for(i in 1:ncells){
    cloglog(psi[i]) <- alpha0 + inprod(alpha[1:ncovs], covs[i, 1:ncovs]) + alpha.car[i]
    log(lambda[i]) <- beta0 + inprod(beta[1:ncovs], covs[i, 1:ncovs]) + beta.car[i]

    N[i] ~ dZIP(lambda[i], zeroProb = (1-psi[i]))
  }

  alpha0 ~ dnorm(0, sd = 10)
  beta0 ~ dnorm(0, sd = 10)
  for(i in 1:ncovs){
    alpha[i] ~ dnorm(0, sd = 10)
    beta[i] ~ dnorm(0, sd = 10)
  }

  #Conditional Auto-Regressive Term
  #https://r-nimble.org/html_manual/cha-spatial.html
  #https://ecosystems.psu.edu/research/labs/walter-lab/manual/chapter-9-spatial-epidemiology-in-winbugs/link-to-pdf
  tau.alpha ~ dgamma(0.01, 0.01)
  alpha.car[1:ncells] ~ dcar_normal(adj = adj[1:nadj], weights = weights[1:nadj], num = num[1:ncells], tau = tau.alpha)

  tau.beta ~ dgamma(0.01, 0.01)
  beta.car[1:ncells] ~ dcar_normal(adj[1:nadj],weights[1:nadj],num[1:ncells], tau.beta)

  ### Observation Process
  #Survey A
  for(j in 1:nsurvey.A){
    E.A[j] <- inprod(gamma.A[1:ncovs.A], covs.A[j,1:ncovs.A])
    p.A[j] <- 1 - (.5)^E.A[j]

    y.A[j] ~ dbinom(size = N[grid.A[j]], prob = p.A[j])
  }
  for(i in 1:ncovs.A){gamma.A[i] ~  T(dnorm(0,0.01), 0,100)}

  #Survey B
  for(j in 1:nsurvey.B){
    E.B[j] <- inprod(gamma.B[1:ncovs.B], covs.B[j,1:ncovs.B])
    p.B[j] <- 1 - (.5)^E.B[j]

    y.B[j] ~ dbinom(size = N[grid.B[j]], prob = p.B[j])
  }
  for(i in 1:ncovs.B){gamma.B[i] ~  T(dnorm(0,0.01), 0,100)}
})

messages.body_plain:
Hi Matt,

For CAR models, I usually suggest excluding the intercept (i.e., alpha0 and beta0 in your case) for the identifiability reasons that John refers to. (I think that is preferable because the zero_mean trick is an ad hoc manipulation within the MCMC, while excluding the intercept avoids the identifiability issue entirely.)

When I did that and played a bit with your "iSDM - Sim Test.R" code, here's what I noticed.
- the regression coefficients seemed to mix reasonably for the most part
- in one run, I noticed the lambdas can shoot off to infinity, presumably because of the log link. So there may be some sensitivity to starting values / random seeds.
- shouldn't you have an intercept in your models for E.A and E.B?

Not a full assessment, but hopefully those thoughts are useful.

-chris

messages.subject: Re: Help to solve the "Dynamic index out of bounds" -warning in runCrossValidate
messages.subject_clean: Help to solve the "Dynamic index out of bounds" -warning in runCrossValidate
messages.body_plain:
Hi Antti,

Sorry about the delay in responding here.

It looks like there are a couple things going on here.

First, it looks like the warning is occurring because of your initialization of `z` for the first time captured. In the original model, you initiate those `z` values in model code. But when you hold out an observation, you are not initiating the `z` for the first time captured for the held-out observations. Try setting `z_inits` as part of `inits`, e.g.,

for(i in 1:nrow(y))
    z_inits[i,first[i]] <- y[i,first[i]]

More generally, I suggest that you not initialize those `z` values in the model code but do it via `inits`.

Second, in the process of looking at this, I realized there was a serious bug in runCrossValidate() affecting the MSE loss function and all user-defined loss functions (but not the 'predictive' loss function) in nimble versions 0.10.0-0.13.1 (starting in October 2020). I'm sending out a separate email about this. The fact that the dynamic index error did not occur for the MSE loss was caused by the bug -- the error should have occurred because of the problem discussed above with the z initialization. Please try rerunning the cross-validation using nimble installed from the devel branch of our GitHub repository or with the forthcoming version 1.0.0.

-chris

messages.subject: runCrossValidate bug in NIMBLE versions 0.10.0 - 0.13.1
messages.subject_clean: runCrossValidate bug in NIMBLE versions 0.10.0 - 0.13.1
messages.body_plain:
We recently uncovered a bug that produces incorrect results when using runCrossValidate() in versions of nimble starting with 0.10.0 (released in October 2020). The bug affects the default MSE loss function and any user-defined loss functions, but not the 'predictive' loss function. Unfortunately the bug caused incorrect MCMC sampling when data were held out, so any cross-validation results obtained with runCrossValidate should be recalculated.

The bug fix will be in our upcoming release of version 1.0.0 and is also included in the development version of NIMBLE on our 'devel' branch, which can be installed from GitHub.

-Chris, for the NIMBLE Development Team

> Hi Chris,
>
> We haven't spent a lot of time fine-tuning `runCrossValidate`, so it's perhaps not too surprising you're running into some bumps.
> Coincidentally, in another recent post <https://groups.google.com/g/nimble-users/c/twcKTbNrUfk>, we had a discussion of clearing compiled objects to release memory.
> To use those strategies, you'd have to modify `nimble:::calcCrossVal`, which is called by `runCrossValidate` and carries out an individual MCMC run.
> Ideally we'd add an argument to `runCrossValidate` so that the compiled objects can be cleared based on that.
>
> As far as the dynamic index out of bounds, nothing obvious is coming to mind as to why that would happen in some of the MCMCs.

messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

First, my apologies if this is not a nimble issue.

I'm working with a large hierarchical model where multiple multivariate normal distributions are fitted to occurrence data. I'm interested in hierarchically modelling the means, SDs, and correlations of these MVN distributions. I'm also interested in comparing these distributions, for which I am using the determinants of the covariance matrices.

For some of these parameters, the covariance matrices are not positive definite, and thus nimble::logdet() gives `NaN`. When I inspect some of the troublesome covariance matrices, I get matrices that are just barely not positive definite. For instance, one original covariance matrix is this:

      [,1]   [,2]   [,3]   [,4]
[1,] 0.145  0.098  0.038  0.084
[2,] 0.098  0.254 -0.150 -0.029
[3,] 0.038 -0.150  0.174  0.116
[4,] 0.084 -0.029  0.116  0.157

which after corpcor::make.positive.definite() becomes (differences in bold):

      [,1]   [,2]   [,3]   [,4]
[1,] 0.146  0.098  0.037  0.084
[2,] 0.098  0.254 -0.150 -0.029
[3,] 0.037 -0.150  0.175  0.116
[4,] 0.084 -0.029  0.116  0.157

The SDs and correlations of this matrix are c(0.381, 0.504, 0.417, 0.397) and c( 0.510, 0.239, 0.557, -0.715, -0.143, 0.701), respectively.

Is there anything I can do ensure the covariance matrices are positive semidefinite? I'm afraid this is beyond my linear algebra skills.

Thanks!

Matt

messages.body_plain:
G'day Perry,

Sure, I normally would use the LKJ priors but for this application I am also interested in hierarchically modeling the correlations, so I'm going the old fashioned way. The code for this stuff is as follows, where i indexes the number of "hypervolumes" and j indexes species:

{
      # means (identity-link)
      mu[i, j, 1:n_dim] <- alpha[1, j, 1:n_dim] + alpha[2, j, 1:n_dim] * equals(i, 2)

      # SDs (log-link)
      sigma[i, j, 1:n_dim] <- exp(beta[1, j, 1:n_dim] + beta[2, j, 1:n_dim] * equals(i, 2))

      # correlations (artanh-link)
      rho[i, j, 1:n_cor] <- nim_tanh(gamma[1, j, 1:n_cor] + gamma[2, j, 1:n_cor] * equals(i, 2))

      # correlation matrix
      Omega[i, j, 1:n_dim, 1:n_dim] <- nim_cor_mat(n_dim, rho[i, j, 1:n_cor])

      # covariance matrix
      Sigma[i, j, 1:n_dim, 1:n_dim] <- diag(sigma[i, j, 1:n_dim]) %*% Omega[i, j, 1:n_dim, 1:n_dim] %*% diag(sigma[i, j, 1:n_dim])

      # likelihood (observation process)
      for (l in 1:n_obs[i, j]) {
        y[i, j, l, 1:n_dim] ~ dmnorm(mu[i, j, 1:n_dim], cov = Sigma[i, j, 1:n_dim, 1:n_dim])
      } # k

      # derived quantities

      # CV (Albert and Zhang 2010)
      CV[i, j] <- nim_cv(mu[i, j, 1:n_dim], Sigma[i, j, 1:n_dim, 1:n_dim])

      # (log) determinants
      log_det[i, j] <- logdet(Sigma[i, j, 1:n_dim, 1:n_dim])

      # variance component of determinants (Lu et al. 2021)
      log_det_var[i, j] <- log(sum(sigma[i, j, 1:n_dim] ^ 2))

      # correlation component of determinants (Lu et al. 2021)
      log_det_cor[i, j] <- log_det[i, j] - log_det_var[i, j]
}

where nim_tanh(), nim_cor_mat(), and nim_cv() are nimbleFunctions for the hyperbolic arctangent, creating a correlation matrix, and calculating a multivariate coefficient of variation.

Cheers,

Matt

messages.body_plain:
Hi Stephanie,
Great to see this and thanks for the question.
All model quantities are doubles, even if in fact their values will be integers. For that reason, please try using "x = double()".
Also, if x is large, it will be better to use lgamma(x + 1) instead of log(factoria(x)).
HTH!
Perry

messages.subject: Re: Help to solve the "Dynamic index out of bounds" -warning in runCrossValidate
messages.subject_clean: Help to solve the "Dynamic index out of bounds" -warning in runCrossValidate
messages.body_plain:
Antti, I had a chance to jump in and take a look at your model.

The good news, I'm happy to report, is that there'ss no error with your model, or nimble's runCrossValidate function.  The process is not getting stuck, it's just takes a (very) long time to do what you're asking.

What's really taking a long time is procedure for estimating the cross validation standard error, which uses bootstrap resampling of the MCMC samples.  By default, runCrossValidate uses 200 bootstrap resamples, and locally on my laptop, each resample takes 5 minutes, so doing all 200 resamples (to estimate the standard error) would take about 16 hours -- for each of the 3 folds.  So this is the main problem.

You could completely turn off the estimation of the CV standard error, by providing the argument "nBootReps = NA" to runCrossValidate.  If you do that, the entire CV routine would take (from my quick estimate) about 5 minutes for each fold, so about 15 minutes total.  This time is driven by the predictive loss function, which requires nontrivial model calculation for each MCMC sample.

If you still desire some estimate of the CV standard error, you can provide a number (smaller than 200) for the nBootReps argument to runCrossValidate.  This would use fewer bootstrap resamples for estimating the CV error, and would give a less accurate estimate of the standard error.

Another approach you could use for speeding up all of these processes, would be to reduce the number of MCMC iterations (n_iter) to lower than 5000.  Everything is scaling according to that, since the bootstrapping process rasamples (and does calculations) proportional to this number, and also the calculation of the CV value itself also scales according to this.  So, you can make the entire process faster (and less accurate) by reducing n_iter.

I hope this helps get you going.  I was glad to not find any errors.  And it was a pleasure working with your extremely tidy code, which I myself also appreciate.

Cheers!
Daniel

messages.subject_clean: LGCP on simulated example
messages.body_plain:
Zhihan, thank you for your message, and apologies for the delay in responding.

Let me say upfront, I have not studied the maths in the Banerjee (2013) paper you sent, so my response is assuming the calculations and theory underlying your llFun are correct.

In the implementation you provided, the "sampling" for the gp_on_knots GP, unfortunately, will not take place conditional on the proposed values of other parameters -- in particular, on sigma, which affect the calculation of the knots_cov.  This might be throwing everything off, and I'm going to suggest a slightly different way of approaching this, essentially, by pushing the calculations, and also the generation of the gp_on_knots GP, into the likelihood function calculation.

A very rough sketch of this would look like:

code <- nimbleCode({
    beta0 ~ dnorm(0, sd = 100)
    beta1 ~ dnorm(0, sd = 100)
    beta2 ~ dnorm(0, sd = 100)
    sigma ~ dinvgamma(1, 1)

})

Rmodel <- nimbleModel(
    code,
    data = list(),

    inits = initial values for the 4 parameters,
    constants = list()
)

llFun <- nimbleFunction(
    setup = function(model,
                     ## all the other constants you need here: covs, sim_covs, knots_dist, the other dist arrays,
                     ## note also that you may not need all of n_uof, n_sim, n_knots for indexing the arrays,
                     ## since arrays do not need to be "fully indexed" in nimbleFunction code.  I'll give an example below.
                     ) { },
    run = function() {
        ## calculate XB
        ## calculate XB_int
        ## calculate knots_cov
        ## calclate observed_pts_vs_knots_cov
        ## calculate integration_pts_vs_knots_cov
        ## *simulate* the GP gp_on_knots:
        knots_cov_chol <- chol(knots_cov)
        gp_on_knots <- rmnorm_chol(1, knots_mean, knots_cov_chol, prec_param = 0)
        ## the above lines first calculate the Cholesky factorization of the covariance matrix,
        ## since nimble's underlying implementation of the multivaraite normal operate
        ## using that.  The argument prec_param = 0 indicates that the third argument (knots_cov_chol)
        ## is the cholesky factor of the covariance matrix (the 0 means "not of the precision matrix")
        ## notice also how we do *not* need indexing such as [1:n_knots] or [1:n_knots, 1:n_knots]
        ## on all the vectors or arrays; omitting the indexing means "use the entire vector or array"
        ## calculate gp_on_observed_pts, again omitting indexing:
        gp_on_observed_pts <- observed_pts_vs_knots_cov %*% inverse(knots_cov) %*% asCol(gp_on_knots)
        ## calculate gp_on_integration_pts
        ## calculate integ
        ll <- sum(XB + gp_on_observed_pts) - integ
        returnType(double())
        return(ll)
    }
)

RllFun <- llFun(Rmodel, all the other constants needed)

mcmcConf <- configureMCMC(Rmodel, nodes = NULL)  ## monitors will be correct by default

mcmcConf$addSampler(target = c("beta0", "beta1", "beta2", "sigma"),
                    type = "RW_llFunction_block",
                    control = list(llFunction = RllFun, includesTarget = FALSE))

## etc....

Does this approach make sense, from the theory standpoint?

If so, there are also some efficiency improvements we could talk about, for pre-calculating some values, caching some values in the model, and certainly also if phi will remain fixed at 4, and probably also relating to the linear algebra calculations involved.

But first, I'm curious if this sounds about right to you, and hear if you have better results using this approach.

Keep in touch, and let me know how it goes.

Cheers,
Daniel

    XB[1:n_uof] <- beta0 + beta1*covs[,1] + beta2*covs[,2]
    XB_int[1:n_sim] <- beta0 + beta1*sim_covs[,1] + beta2*sim_covs[,2]
    knots_cov[1:n_knots, 1:n_knots] <- expcov(knots_dists[1:n_knots, 1:n_knots], phi=4, sigma=sigma)
    observed_pts_vs_knots_cov[1:n_uof, 1:n_knots] <- expcov(observed_pts_vs_knots_dists[1:n_uof, 1:n_knots], phi=4, sigma=sigma)
    integration_pts_vs_knots_cov[1:n_sim, 1:n_knots] <- expcov(integration_pts_vs_knots_dists[1:n_sim, 1:n_knots], phi=4, sigma=sigma)
    gp_on_knots[1:n_knots] ~ dmnorm(knots_mean[1:n_knots], cov=knots_cov[1:n_knots, 1:n_knots])
    gp_on_observed_pts[1:n_uof] <- observed_pts_vs_knots_cov[1:n_uof, 1:n_knots] %*% inverse(knots_cov[1:n_knots, 1:n_knots]) %*% asCol(gp_on_knots[1:n_knots])
    gp_on_integration_pts[1:n_sim] <- integration_pts_vs_knots_cov[1:n_sim, 1:n_knots] %*% inverse(knots_cov[1:n_knots, 1:n_knots]) %*% asCol(gp_on_knots[1:n_knots])
    integ <- (area / n_sim) * sum(exp(XB_int[1:n_sim] + gp_on_integration_pts[1:n_sim]))

> Hi fellow NIMBLE developers,
>
> I’m trying to fit a log-Gaussian Cox process (LGCP) on a simulated dataset, but I’m experiencing problems with MCMC divergence. I’m attempting to use a custom likelihood function. I tried to have separate samplers for each parameter (commented out in my code below), but that also did not work. I would be grateful if you would be willing to take a look and share any thoughts on where/how I might improve my approach. Please let me know if you have any questions!
>
> Thank you very much for your time.
>
> Best,
> Zhihan
>
> Below is a reproducible example in R.
>
> Importing libraries:
>
> ```{r}
>
> set.seed(42)
>
> library(nimble)
>
> library(ggplot2)
>
> library(fields)  # for rdist
>
> library(glue)
>
> library(dplyr)
>
> library(sf)
>
> library(sp)
>
> library(spatstat)
>
> library(reshape2)
>
> #install RandomFieldsUtils if necessary, it has been removed from CRAN
>
> #install.packages(("https://cran.r-project.org/src/contrib/Archive/RandomFieldsUtils/RandomFieldsUtils_1.2.5.tar.gz"), repos=NULL, type="source")
>
> library(RandomFieldsUtils)
>
> #install RandomFields if needed
>
> #install.packages(("https://cran.r-project.org/src/contrib/Archive/RandomFields/RandomFields_3.3.14.tar.gz"), repos=NULL, type="source")
>
> library(RandomFields)
>
> ```
>
> Generate a simulated dataset:
>
> ```{r}
>
> sampled_process <- rLGCP("exp", function(x, y){0.1 * x - 0.1 * y + 1},
>
>            var=1, scale=4,
>
>            win = owin(c(-10, 10), c(-10, 10)))
>
> plot(sampled_process)
>
> ```
>
> I’m using an exponential covariance function:
>
> ```{r}
>
> expcov <- nimbleFunction(run = function(dists = double(2), phi = double(0), sigma = double(0)) {
>
>     returnType(double(2))
>
>     n <- dim(dists)[1]
>
>     m <- dim(dists)[2]
>
>     sigma2 <- sigma*sigma
>
>     result <- sigma2*exp(-dists/phi)
>
>     return(result)
>
> })
>
> ```
>
> Defining observed points (obs_pts), knots and integration points (int_pts):
>
> ```{r}
>
> obs_pts <- as.data.frame(sampled_process)
>
> knots_xs <- seq(from = -10, to = 10, length.out = 10)
>
> knots_ys <- seq(from = -10, to = 10, length.out = 10)
>
> knots <- expand.grid(knots_xs, knots_ys)
>
> colnames(knots) <- c("x", "y")
>
> int_xs <- runif(500, min=-10, max=10)
>
> int_ys <- runif(500, min=-10, max=10)
>
> int_pts <- data.frame(cbind(int_xs, int_ys))
>
> colnames(int_pts) <- c("x", "y")
>
> ```
>
> ```{r}
>
> n_uof = nrow(obs_pts)
>
> n_sim = nrow(int_pts)
>
> n_knots <- nrow(knots)

>
